Vertical exaggeration: 3.0x. 2.2.2 Local Geothermal Conceptual Cross-Section The thermal properties of Puerto Rico have been investigated using both global and site-specific datasets, providing insights into geothermal gradients across the island. Li et al. (2017) developed a global Curie-point depth model through a robust inversion algorithm of magnetic anomaly data based on fractal magnetization, with the dataset made available upon request to the authors.3 Using the Curie-point depth method and the global Curie-point depth EMAG2 database (Li et al. 2017), researchers estimated a regional geothermal gradient of 30°C/km–32°C/km for Puerto Rico. However, local well data indicates lower gradients. Based on geophysical logs from the Toa Baja well, Anderson (1991) interpreted that reburial and deposition of Oligocene-Miocene limestones produced a present-day gradient of about 15°C/km, corresponding to a heat flow of 3 https://www.nature.com/articles/srep45129#Sec12 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 30–50 mW/m². Similarly, direct measurements from well CPR-4 reported a geothermal gradient of 18.5°C/km (Anderson 1991). Together, these findings suggest that while regional models point to elevated geothermal potential, localized lithological and depositional processes and groundwater effects may have resulted in lower gradients in certain areas of Puerto Rico. As a reference for geothermal gradient anomalies in island settings, Wilmarth et al. (2017) reported that geothermal gradients on Tutuila Island are lower than expected for a young volcanic province. They suggested this may result from several factors: the lack of significant magma storage in the shallow crust, the insulating effect of more than 3,000 m of Pleistocene and older shield-volcano basalts that make up much of the island, and the island’s proximity to the near- freezing abyssal plains of the Pacific Ocean only a few kilometers offshore. Together, these conditions help maintain unusually low subsurface temperatures. The geothermal energy investigation of Puerto Rico has been guided by the integration of temperature data with regional geologic and hydrostratigraphic characteristics. Using geothermal gradient estimates derived from Curie-point depth modeling (Li et al. 2017; Lin et al. 2017) and local well measurements (Anderson 1991), combined with a detailed 3D geologic model of the SJMA, researchers developed a conceptual cross section with isotherms extending from south to north near UPR-RP (Figure 11). This conceptual model incorporates the stratigraphic framework of the SJMA, where Quaternary deposits, Oligocene-Miocene limestones, and deeper units such as the Cibao Formation and Mucarabones Sand define a structurally complex aquifer system influenced by tectonic tilting, karstification, and saltwater intrusion. The model emphasizes the interplay of heat flow with hydrostratigraphic units, including the shallow surficial aquifer, the semi-confining clay-rich Cibao facies, and the deeper Mucarabones Sand and lower aquifer system, which together control groundwater movement and thermal distribution. As in Wilmarth (2017) where conceptual cross sections were used to visualize geothermal system components, our Puerto Rico model highlights the influence of lithology and groundwater flow on spatial distribution.
